newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian markets jolted by campaign, Thai woes.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian markets jolted by campaign, Thai woes.

text.p: Sporadic election violence and fears of a meltdown in Thailand jolted Indonesian financial markets on Thursday, economists and dealers said.
The rupiah fell to a low of 2,441 against the dollar in the morning from 2,433.50 at the open.
The stock market suffered similarly, with the composite index falling more than two percent to an intra-day low of 655.74 points at midsession before bouncing back to 656.24 at 0750 GMT.
"Part of the nervousness is related to what happens in the baht. You can see a similar impact on the (Malaysian) ringgit and the (Philippine) peso," an economist with a U.S. bank told Reuters.
A property crisis in Thailand -- which is facing its slowest economic growth in 10 years -- has led to a scrutiny of potential weaknesses in financial markets in the region.
The baht has also come under pressure, forcing the Thai central bank to defend the currency.
Edwin Png, chief treasurer at the Bank of America, said offshore investors were getting nervous because the campaign for the May 29 general elections was becoming increasingly violent.
"There is a spill-over from the Thai baht and they are getting nervous about the election campaign," Png said.
Police said there was minor violence in Jakarta on Wednesday as the Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP) campaigned in the city and in other parts of the main Java island.
Clashes between PPP supporters and police also erupted in Central Java province but there were no casualties and no arrests, they said.

The rupiah tumbled to a low 2,445 in London overnight on false rumours of riots and arson at a police station in Jakarta, but recovered later to 2,435 after police denied there was any major violence.

On Thursday, witnesses said a group of ruling Golkar party supporters clashed with construction site workers in Jakarta after an argument. Several people were injured by stone- throwing, but the fighting soon died down.

The minority PPP and the Christian-Nationalist Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) are battling Golkar for 425 seats in parliament. Another 75 seats in the house are allotted to the military, which does not vote.
Stockbrokers said the fall on the stock market was more related to Thailand although the campaign had definitely added to worries.
"It's the Thai factor I think. If you just see around Asia most markets are pretty much down," said Stephen Doe, research head of PT Asia Equity Jasereh.
He said there were concerns among international investors of oversupply in the Jakarta property market.
"People have concerns about Jakarta. You only have to look out of the window and see a lot of office space being built and just say that there might be one or two problems here," Doe said.
"But we don't think there is a problem. But that is obviously what the international investors are worried about right now," he added.
Brokers said the some investors were looking for bargains in the dips.
"Any time the market has bad days like this it's right to be picking up stocks you like," Doe said.
